text: An orbit that goes around the Earth 8.05 times a day with an eccentricity of 0.25 (the exact 8:1 resonance with the Earth's rotation) is predicted 1.3 km off along its track 7 days after a fit, against 94 to 220 m just either side of it: no part of the model carries that resonance's gravity terms.

On seven real windows of the TESS space telescope (an orbit of 13.7 days that reaches the Moon's distance), predictions from 72-hour fits to its reference's 10-minute states are a median 0.39 km off after one day, 1.9 km after three days and 15.4 km after a week, and 0.81 km ahead of SGP4-XP at three days. The test also holds them to the archived 0.77 km at one day and 7.6 km at a week. That comparison is scored the way the archive was, on a reading in which half the states are a straight-line fill between the reference's states, and there they are 1.01 and 9.0 km. The reference itself steps by 17 to 221 m where it changes from one NASA file to the next, which in six of the seven windows happens 13 hours after the cutoff. TESS fires its thrusters about once a week, by 3 to 11 mm/s. In six of the seven windows a firing lies in the 72-hour fit arc (four windows) or within 13 hours after it (two); 10 mm/s moves the orbit by about 4 km in five days, so past a firing the error measures the firing as much as the prediction.

On a 7-day arc of an eccentric orbit with drag (Molniya), the record states the drag coefficient to 0.09 % while the fitted value is 0.3 to 0.5 % from the truth: the stated uncertainty is 5 to 7 times too small; its position covariance is honest.
